Truce of God Treuga Dei Mandate
Sanctuary Protection for Peasants and Clergy
RagShortTexts: The Truce of God halted feudal feuds from Thursday to Monday, protecting church sanctums.

Variants.Content: The Church launched the Peace of God and the Truce of God in the late tenth and eleventh centuries to restrain the private wars that tore through the countryside. Councils gathered local lords and bishops to swear oaths on relics, promising never to attack unarmed clergy, pilgrims, or peasants, and never to seize draft oxen and farm tools. The Truce of God added time limits: fighting was forbidden from Thursday evening, the hour commemorating the Last Supper, through Monday morning, and throughout Lent. The restrictions tried to protect those who worked the land and travelled the roads, and they set moral limits on the warrior class. Enforcement depended on local bishops and on public oaths, so the movement rested on the willingness of lords to keep their word.
Bishops gathered feuding barons on open fields, demanding solemn oaths of pacification. Breaching the Truce brought immediate anathema, laying early foundations for civilian immunity in warfare.
When parish bells toll on Thursday dusk, serfs breathe relief. Within the consecrated boundary of the churchyard cemetery, armed retainers dare not unsheathe swords without fearing divine judgment.
